quick: 200 mg once daily for 14-day lead-in, then 200 mg twice daily (or 400 mg ER once daily)
With or without food; swallow ER tablets whole
Used in HIV when indicated; high hepatotoxicity risk with higher CD4 counts
Breastfeeding not recommended in HIV (transmission risk)
No adjustment in mild-moderate; supplemental dose after dialysis
LFTs intensively first 18 weeks; skin/rash; never skip lead-in
summary: Nevirapine is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) used in combination antiretroviral therapy for HIV-1 infection. It carries a boxed warning for severe, potentially fatal hepatotoxicity (especially in the first 18 weeks and in patients with higher CD4 counts) and life-threatening skin reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. A mandatory 14-day 200 mg once-daily lead-in reduces rash, after which the dose is escalated.
indications: Treatment of HIV-1 infection in combination with other antiretroviral agents in adults
Treatment of HIV-1 infection in pediatric patients (extended-release: age >=6 years with BSA >=1.17 m2)

dosage.n: First 14 days; do not escalate if rash present

admin: Always begin with the 14-day 200 mg once-daily lead-in to reduce rash risk
Do not escalate the dose if rash or hepatic abnormalities occur during lead-in
Swallow extended-release tablets whole - do not chew, crush, or divide
If dosing interrupted >7 days, restart with the lead-in regimen
moa: Nevirapine binds directly to and non-competitively inhibits HIV-1 reverse transcriptase by binding to an allosteric pocket adjacent to the catalytic site, disrupting the enzyme's polymerase activity. It does not require intracellular phosphorylation and has no significant activity against HIV-2 reverse transcriptase or human DNA polymerases.

absolute: Moderate or severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh B or C)
Use as part of occupational/non-occupational post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) due to hepatotoxicity
Restarting after clinically significant hepatic events or severe rash/hypersensitivity from prior nevirapine
relative: Higher pretreatment CD4 counts (women >250, men >400 cells/mm3) - increased hepatotoxicity risk
Concomitant hepatotoxic drugs or active hepatitis B/C
monitor: Liver function tests, especially first 18 weeks
Symptoms of hypersensitivity (fever, eosinophilia, organ involvement)

preg: Used in HIV-positive pregnant women within combination ART when benefits justify use; however nevirapine should not be initiated in women with CD4 >250 cells/mm3 unless benefit outweighs risk, given heightened symptomatic hepatotoxicity. Monitor liver function closely.
lact: Breastfeeding is not recommended for HIV-infected mothers in settings where safe alternatives exist, because of the risk of HIV transmission and potential adverse effects in the infant.
renal: No dose adjustment is required for mild to moderate renal impairment. In patients on hemodialysis, an additional 200 mg dose following each dialysis session is recommended.
hepatic: Nevirapine is contraindicated in patients with moderate to severe (Child-Pugh B or C) hepatic impairment. Severe and fatal hepatotoxicity can occur; discontinue permanently if clinical hepatitis or transaminase elevations with symptoms develop.

major: Strong CYP3A inducers (rifampin) - reduce nevirapine levels; avoid
Protease inhibitors (atazanavir, lopinavir) - altered concentrations; dose adjustment
Other hepatotoxic agents - additive liver injury
St. John's wort - reduces nevirapine efficacy
moderate: Oral contraceptives (reduced hormonal levels - use additional/alternative contraception)
Azole antifungals (fluconazole increases nevirapine; ketoconazole not recommended)
interactions.food: May be taken without regard to food
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor transaminases (ALT/AST) and bilirubin; may cause elevations

serious: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
emergency: Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN with mucosal involvement

monitoring: Liver function tests at baseline, frequently during the first 18 weeks, then periodically
Clinical and laboratory monitoring intensively during the first 8 weeks
Skin examination for rash, particularly during lead-in
Symptoms of hypersensitivity (fever, blistering, oral lesions, facial edema)
CD4 count and HIV-1 RNA for therapeutic response
counsel: Never skip the 14-day lead-in dosing - it lowers the risk of severe rash
Stop the drug and seek care immediately for rash, blistering, mouth sores, fever, or yellowing of eyes/skin
Report dark urine, severe fatigue, nausea, or right upper abdominal pain (liver warning signs)
Use a barrier or alternative contraceptive method - nevirapine can reduce the pill's effectiveness
Take exactly as prescribed and do not run out of medicine; missing doses can cause resistance
Avoid alcohol and other liver-toxic substances
pk: Rapidly absorbed; antiviral effect develops with steady-state combination therapy
Plasma peak about 4 hours after an oral immediate-release dose
Approximately 25-30 hours at steady state (auto-induces its own metabolism)
Long half-life allows once- or twice-daily dosing
Store at 25 C (excursions 15-30 C); protect from excess moisture
pearls: Boxed warning: severe/fatal hepatotoxicity and skin reactions, highest in first 18 weeks
Mandatory 14-day 200 mg once-daily lead-in markedly reduces rash incidence
Do not start in women with CD4 >250 or men with CD4 >400 cells/mm3 unless benefit outweighs risk
Auto-induces CYP3A4/2B6, lowering its own and co-administered drug levels
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as remembered, then continue the usual schedule; do not double up. If therapy has been interrupted for more than 7 days, restart with the 14-day 200 mg once-daily lead-in.
overdose: There is no antidote. Reported overdose effects include edema, erythema nodosum, fatigue, fever, headache, insomnia, nausea, pulmonary infiltrates, rash, vertigo, vomiting, and weight loss, which resolve on withdrawal. Treatment is supportive.
